title: What is this? — demonstratives, articles and the plural
goal: Point at things and name them, choose between *a* and *az*, and form plurals with *-k* — while enjoying one big saving: Hungarian nouns have no grammatical gender.
bekal: use *a* and *az* in the right place, including in the pattern *ez a könyv*
form the plural, and know when an adjective follows suit and when it does not

dialogs.title: Dialogue — A könyvesboltban
dialogs.intro: Budi walks into a small bookshop in Budapest, looking for a dictionary. The shopkeeper is patient.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: And that? Is that a dictionary too?

lines.speaker: Eladó:
lines.text: Nem, az egy nyelvkönyv. Nagyon jó könyv.
lines.id: No, that is a language textbook. A very good book.
lines.literal: no, that a language-book. very good book.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: And all these? Are these dictionaries too?

lines.speaker: Eladó:
lines.text: Nem, ezek nem szótárak. Ezek térképek.
lines.id: No, these are not dictionaries. These are maps.
lines.literal: no, these not dictionaries. these maps.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I see. And what is over there?

lines.speaker: Eladó:
lines.text: Ott vannak a regények és az újságok.
lines.id: Over there are novels and newspapers.
lines.literal: there they-are the novels and the newspapers.

lines.speaker: Eladó:
lines.text: Igen, az egy nagyon jó regény. Magyar író.
lines.id: Yes, it is a very good novel. The author is Hungarian.
lines.literal: yes, that a very good novel. Hungarian author.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Thank you. I'll take this book.

notes: **Ez mi?** — two words with no verb, word for word "this what?". The order can be flipped to *Mi ez?* and the meaning does not change; only the emphasis does. Hungarian is very flexible about word order, but not random — the most important part always sits **right before the verb**.

**Az does two jobs.** *Az* means "that", and *az* is also "the" before a word that starts with a vowel. The sentence tells them apart, and Hungarians are never confused by it. You won't be either, after a few days.

**Ez a könyv, not ez könyv.** When a demonstrative stands in front of a noun, the article is **required**: *ez a könyv* (this book), *az a ház* (that house). Literally "this the book". Dropping *a* there is the quickest-to-spot beginner mistake.

**Egy means "one" and "a/an" at once.** It is used when something is introduced for the first time: *Ez egy szótár*. Once the thing is known, it becomes *a szótár*. In many sentences *egy* can simply be dropped — *Ez szótár* is still correct, just flatter.

**The plural is formed with -k, and almost always needs a linking vowel.** *könyv* → *könyv**ek***, *szótár* → *szótár**ak***, *térkép* → *térkép**ek***. Words that already end in a vowel just add *-k*: *ajtó* → *ajtók*.

grammars.title: Ez és az — this and that
body: Just four forms, and no gender to match.

head: Magyar
Say it
Meaning
Example
rows: *Ez egy könyv.* = This is a book.
*Az egy ház.* = That is a house.

after: When the demonstrative stands alone as the subject, the structure is straight: *Ez egy szótár.*

When it describes a noun, the structure changes and **the article is required**: *ez a szótár* (this dictionary), *azok a könyvek* (those books). Note that the demonstrative becomes plural too, while the article does not.
That structure may feel redundant to an English speaker — as if you were saying "this the dictionary". Accept it as the standard form; there is no other correct way.

grammars.title: A and az — one article, two forms
body: Like *a* and *an* in English, the choice is decided by the first sound of the word that follows — not by meaning, not by gender.
after: Hungarian uses the definite article quite often. Country names take it (*a Magyarország* — except in many fixed phrases), and so do times and general things. If in doubt at A1: **use a/az when it is clear which one you mean**, and drop it when you are speaking in general.
This article will also decide the verb form later, in Unit 11. So paying attention to it now is not a matter of neatness, but an investment.

grammars.title: The plural: -k and its linking vowel
body: Just one letter marks the plural. All you have to choose is the vowel that bridges to it — and the choice follows the vowel harmony from Unit 2.
after: **Watch a and e at the end of a word.** Both **lengthen** as soon as an ending is added: *alma* → *almák*, *kutya* → *kutyák*, *fekete* → *feketék*. This rule applies to all endings, not only the plural, and it is one of the most often forgotten.

**A handful of back-vowel words take -ak, not -ok.** There are few of them and they are best memorized outright: *ház* → *házak*, *fal* → *falak*, *toll* → *tollak*, *hal* → *halak*, *út* → *utak*. Note that the long vowel of *út* shortens in *utak* — this group of words likes to misbehave.

blocks.text: All the words below are written together with their article, so the choice of *a* or *az* gets memorized with no extra effort.
Note that *ceruza* and *táska* end in a vowel, so the plural just adds *-k* — after the *a* lengthens to *á*.

sections.title: Adjectives: before the noun and at the end of the sentence

blocks.text: This is the one place in this unit that really needs your attention, because English adjectives never change for number, so nothing here is familiar.

head: Position of the adjective
Takes the plural?
Example
rows: **At the end** of the sentence, as a predicate

blocks.text: So *piros* in *a piros könyvek* stays as it is, but *piros* in *A könyvek pirosak* must be plural. How to remember it: an adjective attached to a noun rides on the noun's plural; an adjective standing alone must carry its own plural.

blocks.title: More adjectives that are useful right away
items: Note the last two: *könnyű* and *nehéz* each do two jobs at once, just as English can call a task "light" or "heavy" as well as an object.
